# opencode-sandbox

[![CI](https://github.com/Hamza-Abili/opencode-sandbox/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/Hamza-Abili/opencode-sandbox/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/%40hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox)
[![npm downloads](https://img.shields.io/npm/dt/%40hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox)
[![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/Hamza-Abili/opencode-sandbox?style=social)](https://github.com/Hamza-Abili/opencode-sandbox/stargazers)
[![license](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)](https://github.com/Hamza-Abili/opencode-sandbox/blob/main/LICENSE)

**Native command sandbox for OpenCode V1 and V2.**

Every shell command runs inside the OS sandbox: [bubblewrap](https://github.com/containers/bubblewrap)
on Linux and **Seatbelt** (`sandbox-exec`) on macOS — unless the trusted policy
explicitly authorizes that exact command through `unsandboxedCommands`, or the
global `mode: "permissive"` opt-out is set. The workspace is writable, the
system is read-only, `$HOME` is synthetic, ambient secrets are cleared, and the
network is denied by default. **Fail-closed**: if the sandbox cannot be created,
commands are refused — never silently run unsandboxed.

Zero runtime dependencies. No helper daemon. No proxy. No SRT.

Security policy comes from a **trusted file outside the workspace**. A
repository's `opencode.json` can only tighten it, never set `network: "allow"`,
add `~/.ssh` as readable, pass a provider token, or disable the tool guard
(once the plugin is loaded; see the plugin-removal limitation below).
OpenCode/Git configuration and execution hooks (`.opencode`, `opencode.json`,
`.git/hooks`, `.git/config`, `.envrc`) are read-only inside the sandbox, so a
prompt-injected command cannot persist code that runs on the host after a
restart or `git commit` through those existing paths. Platform limits
(macOS rename/hardlinks, Linux missing paths) are documented below.

On V2, an in-process tool guard applies the same workspace policy to OpenCode's
file tools and `webfetch`, including a hostname allowlist. It is a policy layer,
not a second OS sandbox; see [Tool guard](#tool-guard-v2).

The V2 path uses `ctx.shell.hook("create.before")` and replaces **only the
shell executable** with a generated wrapper. The command, working directory,
timeout, permission rules and session history keep their original values.
The V1 path uses the legacy `tool.execute.before` hook; see [V1](#opencode-v1)
for its documented limitations.

## Requirements

- **Linux**: `bubblewrap` installed system-wide. Debian/Ubuntu:
  `sudo apt install bubblewrap`.
  On Ubuntu 24.04+ unprivileged user namespaces are restricted by AppArmor;
  enable the `bwrap-userns-restrict` profile as documented by bubblewrap.
- **macOS**: built-in `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec` (Seatbelt). Works on current
  macOS releases; the CI matrix runs the real macOS integration tests on a
  GitHub macOS runner.
- **Windows**: run OpenCode inside **WSL2**. The WSL distro is a normal Linux
  host, so bubblewrap and this plugin work unchanged. Keep projects under the
  Linux filesystem (`~/...`, not `/mnt/c/...`) for correct permissions and
  performance. Native Windows (PowerShell) is not supported and fails closed;
  it would need a native helper backend, which is outside this zero-dependency
  package.

The plugin probes a **real** sandbox at startup and reports the exact failure
instead of assuming the binary is usable. The sandbox binary is resolved from
fixed root-owned absolute locations, never through `PATH`.

### Windows via WSL2

Native Windows is not supported. Use WSL2, where OpenCode is a normal Linux
process:

1. Install OpenCode **inside the WSL distro**, not on Windows.
2. `sudo apt install bubblewrap`. On Ubuntu 24.04+, install/enable the
   `bwrap-userns-restrict` AppArmor profile (see the bubblewrap documentation).
3. Keep projects under the Linux filesystem (`~/src/...`), not `/mnt/c/...`.
4. Verify with `bunx --bun @hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox doctor`.
5. Start OpenCode from the WSL shell. If you use the Desktop app, point it at
   the WSL server as usual; the sandbox runs where the server runs.

The startup log adds `wsl=<distro>` when it detects WSL. `doctor` reports the
same and points at the AppArmor/userns check when the probe fails.

## Install (OpenCode V2)

Add the plugin to your config. Security options do **not** belong here; see
[Trusted policy](#trusted-policy).

```jsonc
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "plugins": ["@hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox"]
}
```

Restart OpenCode. On load the plugin logs:

```
[opencode-sandbox] ready (platform=linux, sandbox=bwrap, network=deny, mode=enforce, toolGuard=enforce,
webfetch=allow, workspace=/path/to/project, protected=14, denied=0, unsandboxed=0)
```

If you run OpenCode inside WSL2, the same line adds `wsl=<distro>`.
`protected` and `denied` count policy entries, not necessarily active mounts
(Linux cannot bind a missing protected path).

## Install (OpenCode V1)

V1 uses the same package; the default export exposes both `setup()` for V2 and
`server()` for V1. Enable it with the V1 plugin list:

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": ["@hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox"]
}
```

### OpenCode V1

V1 has no shell-executable hook. The adapter rewrites the command string to

```
'/path/to/opencode-sandbox-wrapper' -c '<original command>'
```

The sandbox boundary is identical, and the wrapper re-validates the real
working directory. The limitation is V1's own parser: OpenCode V1 evaluates
its permission rules and records history against the rewritten command string,
not the original one, so command-level deny/ask rules on the original command
are not preserved. The V1 tool guard checks file arguments (including
`apply_patch`) and the initial `webfetch` URL, but V1 has no redirect hook.
Use V2 when permission-rule fidelity matters. The adapter is tested against
OpenCode 1.19.5. The V2 path is contract-checked against the OpenCode v2 plugin
API (tested on 2.3.0; the package declares `>=1.19 <2 || >=2.0`). A V1 wrapper
replay is identified by OpenCode's call ID, not by trusting a command string
that merely starts with the wrapper prefix.

## Trusted policy

Security-widening settings are read only from files outside the workspace:

| Scope | Path |
| --- | --- |
| User | `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/opencode-sandbox.json`, or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json`, or `~/.config/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json` |
| System (Linux) | `/etc/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json` |
| System (macOS) | `/Library/Application Support/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json` |

The system file must be root-owned; user and system files must not be
group/world-writable or inside the workspace. Keep the user file outside paths
the sandbox can write (on macOS, not under `/tmp` or `/var/folders`). Invalid
JSON, unknown keys, and malformed values make the plugin **ignore that file**.
If a **system** policy is present but invalid, the user file is ignored too and
the secure defaults apply, so an administrator typo cannot silently remove the
cap. Errors are logged. The file is strict JSON (no comments).

The user file may widen the defaults; the system file is a complete baseline
that caps the user file; plugin options can only tighten the result. This is
the precedence:

```
defaults (deny network, enforce, cleared env)
  → user trusted file        may widen
  → system trusted file      may only cap
  → plugin options           may only tighten
```

A `network: "allow"`, `mode: "permissive"`, `toolGuard: "off"`, `writablePaths`,
`readablePaths`, `passEnv`, `shell`, `deniedPaths`, or
`unsandboxedCommands` in a repository's `opencode.json` is ignored with a
warning. To use one, put it in the trusted file.

Example `~/.config/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json`:

```json
{
  "network": "allow",
  "writablePaths": ["/tmp/build-cache"],
  "readablePaths": ["~/.config/gh"],
  "passEnv": ["NODE_OPTIONS"]
}
```

### Migrating from 0.2.x

If a repository or your OpenCode config used `network: "allow"`,
`mode: "permissive"`, `toolGuard: "off"`, `writablePaths`, `readablePaths`,
`passEnv`, `shell`, `deniedPaths` or `unsandboxedCommands` in the plugin entry,
move those values to the trusted user file. From 0.3.0 they are ignored with a
warning; tightening values (`network: "deny"`, `mode: "enforce"`,
`toolGuard: "enforce"`, `webfetch: "deny"`, `webfetchAllowlist`) keep working
in the plugin entry. A symlinked `.git/hooks` directory must be replaced with a
real directory; it is rejected at setup.

### Options

| Option | Type | Default | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `network` | `"deny" \| "allow"` | `"deny"` | `deny` removes the network namespace (Linux) / denies all network operations (macOS). `allow` shares the host network. There is intentionally no shell-network domain allowlist: a real one needs a TLS-intercepting proxy, which would add a dependency and a certificate authority to trust. `webfetchAllowlist` is a separate application-level hostname filter for the `webfetch` tool, not a proxy and not shell egress. |
| `mode` | `"enforce" \| "permissive"` | `"enforce"` | `enforce` refuses shell commands when the sandbox is unavailable. `permissive` runs shell commands unsandboxed with a warning. Explicit opt-out only. |
| `writablePaths` | `string[]` | `[]` | Extra host paths read-write inside the sandbox. Must exist; canonicalised (symlinks resolved); `/`, the host home and its ancestors, credential directories and host system paths are rejected. A path cannot also be listed in `readablePaths`. |
| `readablePaths` | `string[]` | `[]` | Extra host paths read-only inside the sandbox. Root, host home and ancestors are rejected; explicit credential/system paths are allowed read-only as a trust decision. A more specific readable path overrides a broader writable mount; the workspace and any path also listed as writable are rejected. |
| `passEnv` | `string[]` | `[]` | Environment variables copied from the plugin process into the sandbox. Reserved keys (`HOME`, `PATH`, `TMPDIR`, `XDG_*`, …) cannot be overridden. |
| `shell` | `string` | `/bin/bash` (or `/bin/sh`) | Absolute shell used **inside** the sandbox. |
| `toolGuard` | `"enforce" \| "off"` | `"enforce"` | V2 in-process policy for file tools and `webfetch`. It reuses the same workspace, `writablePaths` and `readablePaths`, resolves symlinks and denies paths outside that policy. `off` disables the whole in-process layer; `webfetch: "deny"` and `webfetchAllowlist` then require `"enforce"` and are rejected. This is a policy layer, not an OS boundary; see [Tool guard](#tool-guard-v2). |
| `webfetch` | `"allow" \| "deny"` | `"allow"` | `deny` blocks every `webfetch` call. Requires `toolGuard: "enforce"`. |
| `webfetchAllowlist` | `string[]` | `[]` | If non-empty, only these hostnames are allowed. `*.example.com` matches the apex and subdomains. The `webfetch` tool checks every redirect through the same hook on V2; `image_generate` checks only its initial image URL. Requires `toolGuard: "enforce"`. |
| `deniedPaths` | `string[]` | `[]` | Paths hidden from the sandbox. Existing files are masked (including files in system roots such as `/etc/hosts`), existing directories become empty tmpfs mounts (writes there are ephemeral), and the tool guard denies reads and writes, including missing paths resolved through the nearest existing ancestor and broken final symlink targets. Relative paths resolve against the workspace. On Linux a missing or broken target cannot be masked until it exists; the tool guard still denies it. Trusted policy only. |
| `unsandboxedCommands` | `string[]` | `[]` | Exact commands or `prefix *` patterns that run outside the sandbox. A `prefix *` pattern authorizes **all arguments** of that command, and the command runs with the host environment and cwd; keep entries exact where possible. The matcher rejects `;`, `&`, `\|`, backtick, `$`, `(`, `)`, `<`, `>`, and newlines, so an entry cannot authorize a chained command. Logged in `OSB_TRACE` by pattern index. Trusted policy only. |

Plugin options (the `options` object on the plugin entry) are still accepted
for **tightening only**: `network: "deny"`, `mode: "enforce"`,
`toolGuard: "enforce"`, `webfetch: "deny"` or `webfetchAllowlist`. Everything
else is ignored with a warning. Put security policy in the trusted file.

Paths are canonicalised when the layout is built. Missing paths are an error,
not a silent skip: a sandbox with a mistyped mount would otherwise look
protected while the path is invisible. Writable host system paths are rejected;
projects under `/opt`, `/usr/local`, `/System`, `/Library`, `/nix/store`, `/run`
or a protected `/var` subtree must be moved (read-only access can be granted
with `readablePaths`). `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`, `/private/var/tmp`, `/var/folders`,
`/private/var/folders` and `/var/www` are the explicit writable exceptions.
`/var/www` is a convenience exception: do not mount it writable if a host web
server executes files from that tree.

Mounts are applied from the broadest to the narrowest path. A more specific
mount wins: the workspace and `writablePaths` are read-write, `readablePaths`
are read-only, including when they are a subdirectory of the workspace. A
readable path that is only an ancestor of the workspace does not make the
workspace read-only. The same path cannot be both writable and readable, and
the workspace cannot be listed as readable; such a configuration is rejected
at setup.

## What is sandboxed

- **All shell-service commands on V2**: the agent's `shell` tool and the
  terminal/TUI shell both go through `Shell.create`, which is where the hook
  is installed.
- **V1**: the agent's `bash` tool (`shell` on newer V1 builds). The terminal
  shell bypasses the V1 tool hook; that is a V1 API limitation.
- **Filesystem (Linux)**: only the system runtime (`/usr`, `/bin`, `/sbin`,
  `/lib*`, `/etc`, `/usr/local`, `/opt`, `/nix/store`), the runtime mounts
  (`/proc`, `/dev`, a private `/tmp` and `/run`), a synthetic `/home/sandbox`
  and the explicitly allowed paths are visible. The workspace is read-write;
  everything else is read-only or invisible; the host home is not mounted.
- **Filesystem (macOS)**: Seatbelt allowlist for the system runtime, the
  workspace, the synthetic home and explicit paths. Contents of the host home
  are denied (metadata is still readable); writes are limited to the workspace,
  synthetic home (including its `tmp`) and explicit writable paths; host temp
  dirs are not visible. `TMPDIR` points at the synthetic home temp.
- **Environment**: cleared and rebuilt from `PATH`, `TERM`, locale, `TZ`, a
  synthetic `HOME` plus `passEnv`. `--clearenv` is used on Linux; `env -i` on
  macOS.
- **Process**: `--unshare-all`, `--cap-drop ALL`, `--die-with-parent`,
  `--new-session` (Linux); Seatbelt confinement is inherited by every child
  (macOS).
- **Network**: denied by default.
- **Workspace config**: `.opencode`, `opencode.json`, `opencode.jsonc`,
  `.claude`, `.agents`, `.git/config`, `.git/config.worktree`, `.git/hooks`,
  `.git/info/attributes`, `.git/modules`, `.git/worktrees`, `.gitmodules`, `.gitattributes` and
  `.envrc` are readable but not writable inside the sandbox. Existing
  linked-worktree `config.worktree` files are covered too. The tool guard also
  denies writes to paths that do not exist yet. Every symlink inside a
  repository-controlled protected tree (`.opencode`, `.claude`, `.agents`) is
  rejected at setup; a real `node_modules` directory is skipped, but a symlink
  named `node_modules` is rejected. A protected path with a symlinked parent is
  rejected. A bounded workspace scan protects every existing nested `.git`
  entry: submodule pointer files, absorbed worktrees and nested repositories.
  A `.git` file pointer may target the main repository's `.git/modules` or
  `.git/worktrees` outside the workspace (outside the sandbox and not inside a
  writable mount); a pointer to another in-workspace path outside those trees,
  a pointer whose raw path traverses a mutable workspace child, or one into a
  configured writable mount, is rejected. Symlinks inside a nested `.git` are
  rejected. The root `.git` stays
  writable for Git; the fi

  command can create e.g. a new `opencode.json`; on macOS this gap does not

- macOS Seatbelt rules are **path-based**. The profile denies `file-link` to

## Why this one

| | opencode-sandbox (V1) | this plugin |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenCode V2 | ❌ ([#91](https://github.com/isanchez31/opencode-sandbox-plugin/issues/91)) | ✅ native `ctx.shell.hook` |
| OpenCode V1 | ✅ | ✅ legacy adapter |
| Runtime dependencies | `@anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime` | **zero** |
| Linux engine | bwrap via SRT | bwrap directly |
| macOS engine | Seatbelt via SRT | Seatbelt profile generated natively |
| V2 permissions/history | n/a | original command preserved |
| Network | proxy + domain allowlist | deny or allow (no proxy) |
| Policy trust | project config can weaken it | trusted file outside the workspace; project config only tightens |
| Workspace config | writable | `.opencode`, `opencode.json`, Git hooks/config, `.envrc` read-only |
| Secret paths | deny list | masked `deniedPaths` + tool-guard denial |
| Defaults | permissive/enforce modes | fail-closed, network denied, env cleared |

The project deliberately stays small: the shell is OS-sandboxed, file tools and
`webfetch` get a boundary policy in the server process, and there is no
management UI, proxy, credential vault or container runtime.

## Whole-process sandboxes (nono, OpenShell)

Tools such as [nono](https://nono.sh/docs/cli/clients/opencode) and
[OpenShell](https://docs.nvidia.com/openshell/) run the whole agent inside the
boundary and therefore cover more than this plugin: file tools, MCP, LSP,
`webfetch` and the rest of the process. The tradeoff is the launch model.

As of November 2026, nono's V2 docs call for `--standalone` when you need full
containment: OpenCode normally connects its client to a background daemon that
owns tool execution, plugins and model requests. Sandboxing only the client
leaves that daemon outside the boundary. Launching a fresh daemon inside the
same sandbox meets the containment goal. nono's profile has also used
`OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1` as a startup workaround; that behavior can
change as OpenCode fixes project discovery, so check the current profile.
OpenShell runs the agent in a container with a gateway, network proxy and
credential policy.

This plugin does not relaunch OpenCode: it stays a server plugin, so project
configuration and Desktop's local server keep working. Choose whole-process
containment when you need it; choose this plugin when you want OS-sandboxed
shell commands plus an in-process tool policy without changing how OpenCode is
launched. They are complementary, and the shell boundary here can be layered
under a whole-process sandbox.

## Verification

The integration suite runs real sandboxes; unit tests use fakes only for host
surfaces that are not the sandbox itself:

- Linux: workspace writes, host-path denial, host-home invisibility, environment
  scrubbing, network denial, extra mount opt-in, readable/writable mount
  precedence, working-directory handling and wrapper escape refusal.
- macOS: the same suite on a real GitHub macOS runner via `/usr/bin/sandbox-exec`.
- Policy trust: a hostile `opencode.json` cannot widen the sandbox; a trusted
  file can; malformed/unsafe policy files are ignored in favour of defaults.
- Workspace hardening: `.opencode`, `opencode.json`, Git hooks/config and
  `.envrc` are read-only; `deniedPaths` are hidden; normal writes still work.
- Live smoke: an ephemeral `opencode serve` runs a real shell command through the
  V2 hook, asserts the tool guard is registered and history kept the original
  command, verifies a host-home secret and the server password stay outside

publish.

## Diagnostics

The package ships a non-destructive doctor. It creates and removes a temporary
runtime directory for the probe (and may create the user cache directory if it
is absent), but does not modify the workspace or policy. It prints the
platform/WSL state, the trusted policy files and their `active`/`invalid`/
`absent` status, the effective policy, mount counts, the trusted binary and a
**real generated-wrapper probe** with the configured shell. It never starts a
model or a server:

```bash
bunx --bun @hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox doctor
bunx --bun @hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox doctor --json
bunx --bun @hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox doctor --workspace /path/to/project
```

Exit codes: `0` ready, `1` policy/layout/probe problem, `2` usage error. The
doctor needs Bun (OpenCode's own runtime); it does not start a model or a
server. It never prints environment values; `--json` includes local paths and
environment variable names but not `unsandboxedCommands` values.

## 0.3.0 — trusted policy and workspace hardening

Security release. Versions up to and including 0.2.1 read security policy from
the merged OpenCode plugin options, which a repository's own `opencode.json`
can override. A cloned repository could therefore set `network: "allow"`,
`mode: "permissive"`, `toolGuard: "off"`, add `~/.ssh` as readable, or pass a
provider token. A sandboxed command could also write `.opencode/plugin/*.ts`,
`.git/hooks`, `opencode.json` or `.envrc`, which a host process executes later.

- **Trusted policy outside the workspace.** Widening options are read only from
  `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/opencode-sandbox.json` (default
  `~/.config/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json`) and the root-owned system file
  (`/etc/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json` on Linux,
  `/Library/Application Support/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json` on macOS).
  The system file caps the user file; plugin options can only tighten the
  result. Invalid, unknown-key, group/world-writable, foreign-owned, or
  workspace-local policy files are ignored with an error, never partially
  applied. A present-but-invalid **system** file also disables the user file,
  so an administrator typo cannot remove the cap.
- **Protected workspace config.** `.opencode`, `opencode.json`,
  `opencode.jsonc`, `.claude`, `.agents`, `.git/config`,
  `.git/config.worktree`, `.git/hooks`, `.git/info/attributes`, `.git/modules`, `.git/worktrees`,
  `.gitmodules`, `.gitattributes` and `.envrc` are read-only inside the
  sandbox and write-denied by the tool guard. Existing linked-worktree
  `config.worktree` files are covered. Any symlink inside a
  repository-controlled protected tree (`.opencode`, `.claude`, `.agents`) is
  rejected at setup; a real `node_modules` directory is skipped, but a symlink
  named `node_modules` is rejected, and a protected path with a symlinked
  parent is rejected. A bounded workspace scan protects every existing nested
  `.git` entry (submodule pointer files, absorbed worktrees, nested
  repositories). A `.git` pointer to the main repository's `.git/modules` or
  `.git/worktrees` outside the workspace is allowed (not writable); a pointer
  to another in-workspace path outside those trees, through a mutable workspace
  child, or into a writable mount is rejected. The file tools refuse writes to
  any nested `.git` while the root `.git` stays writable.
  `.git/hooks`/`.git/modules`/`.git/worktrees` roots are protected but not
  recursively scanned.
  A symlinked `.git/hooks` directory is rejected at setup.
  On Linux, `.git` is pinned as a mountpoint (rename-proof) and explicit
  read-only `.git/...` mounts keep precedence. macOS denies the `.git` and
  protected directory entries against rename and denies `file-link` to
  protected/denied paths. This closes the existing-path "plant a plugin/hook
  and wait for restart/commit" escalation; platform residuals are listed
  below.
- **Tool-guard temp reads removed.** Host `<os.tmpdir>/opencode` and OpenCode's
  retained `tool-output` directory are no longer automatic read roots. They can
  contain other sessions' images or truncated output; add one to
  `readablePaths` if needed. This also keeps the macOS tool guard consistent
  with the shell's host-temp isolation.
- **`deniedPaths`.** Trusted-only list of paths hidden from the sandbox
  (`read` and `write` denied). Existing files are masked, including system
  roots; existing directories become empty tmpfs mounts; a denied parent masks
  a writable child; missing paths under symlinked parents and broken final
  symlink targets are resolved through the nearest existing ancestor. On Linux
  a missing/broken target cannot be masked until it exists; the tool guard still
  denies it. Use it for `.env`, `secrets/` and similar.
- **`unsandboxedCommands`.** Trusted-only exact/`prefix *` commands that run
  on the host. The matcher rejects `;`, `&`, `|`, backtick, `$`, `(`, `)`,
  `<`, `>` and newlines, so an entry cannot authorize a chained command. A
  `prefix *` entry authorizes all arguments and the command inherits the host
  environment and cwd. Matches are logged by pattern index, never with the
  command or pattern text.
- **macOS host temp isolation.** Host `/tmp`, `/private/tmp`, `/var/folders`
  and `/private/var/folders` are neither readable nor writable; the synthetic
  home's `tmp` is `TMPDIR`. Workspace symlinks to the host home or host temp
  are denied by resolved-path rules; integration tests cover reads and writes.
- **WSL2.** Windows is supported through WSL2; the startup log reports the WSL
  distro and native `win32` fails closed with a WSL2 hint. The doctor reports
  the same and points at the AppArmor/userns check.
- **`doctor`.** `bunx --bun @hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox doctor [--json]` prints
  the platform/WSL state, trusted policy status, effective policy, mount
  counts, trusted binary and a real **generated-wrapper** probe (including the
  configured shell). Exit codes are 0/1/2.
- **V1 replay safety.** A caller-supplied command that starts with the
  generated wrapper prefix is refused instead of trusted. A replay is accepted
  only when both the OpenCode call ID and the exact rewritten command match;
  a fresh command under an old call ID is wrapped again (or refused if it
  claims to be a wrapper). This closes a V1 host escape available from the
  command string recorded in history.
- **Tests.** 216 tests, including a live smoke with a hostile project config,
  protected/denied integration on real bwrap/Seatbelt, policy precedence,
  unsafe-file rejection, unsandboxed pattern matching and WSL detection.
- **Migration (breaking).** Move `network: "allow"`, `mode: "permissive"`,
  `toolGuard: "off"`, `writablePaths`, `readablePaths`, `passEnv`, `shell`,
  `deniedPaths` and `unsandboxedCommands` from the plugin entry to the trusted
  user file. Tightening values can stay in the plugin entry. The plugin logs a
  warning for each ignored widening option.

- A project config can still **remove** the plugin

- A nested repository with its own checked-out submodules/worktrees is not

- `.git/hooks` and `.git/modules` are protected as roots but not recursively

  nested `.gitattributes` files are not contained. New `file-link` calls to

# Security

The product **is** the boundary. Treat every claim here as load-bearing.

## Model

- **Default deny.** `network` defaults to `"deny"`; the sandbox starts from an
  empty mount namespace (Linux) or a deny-default Seatbelt profile (macOS).
  Only the system runtime, the workspace, a synthetic home and explicit extra
  mounts are visible.
- **No ambient secrets.** The environment is cleared (`--clearenv` on Linux,
  `env -i` on macOS) and rebuilt from a small allowlist plus `passEnv`.
  Provider tokens and host secrets do not reach commands unless the user
  explicitly passes them.
- **Trusted policy outside the workspace.** Security-widening settings
  (`network: "allow"`, `mode: "permissive"`, `toolGuard: "off"`,
  `writablePaths`, `readablePaths`, `passEnv`, `shell`, `deniedPaths`,
  `unsandboxedCommands`) are read only from
  `$OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR/opencode-sandbox.json` (default
  `~/.config/opencode/opencode-sandbox.json`) or the root-owned system file.
  A repository's `opencode.json` can only tighten the result. Trusted files
  that are invalid JSON, contain unknown keys, are group/world-writable, are
  owned by another user, or live inside the workspace are ignored in favour of
  the secure defaults. Keep the user file outside sandbox-writable temp
  directories (on macOS, not under `/tmp` or `/var/folders`); the default
  `~/.config/opencode` is outside the sandbox. If the **system** file is
  present but invalid, the user file is ignored too, so an administrator typo
  cannot remove the cap. The system file is a complete baseline that caps the
  user file.
- **Protected workspace config.** A sandboxed command can write the workspace
  but not the files a host process executes later: `.opencode`,
  `opencode.json`, `opencode.jsonc`, `.claude`, `.agents`, `.git/config`,
  `.git/config.worktree`, `.git/hooks`, `.git/info/attributes`, `.git/modules`, `.git/worktrees`,
  existing `.git/worktrees/*/config.worktree` files, `.gitattributes`,
  `.gitmodules` and `.envrc`. Existing paths are read-only mounts (Linux) or
  write-denied by Seatbelt (macOS); the tool guard refuses writes even to paths
  that do not exist yet. Every symlink inside a repository-controlled protected
  tree (`.opencode`, `.claude`, `.agents`) is rejected at setup; a real
  `node_modules` directory is skipped, but a symlink named `node_modules` is
  rejected, and a protected path with a symlinked parent is rejected. A
  bounded workspace scan protects every existing nested `.git` entry: submodule
  pointer files, absorbed worktrees and nested repositories. A `.git` pointer
  may target the main repository's `.git/modules` or `.git/worktrees` outside
  the workspace (outside the sandbox and not inside a writable mount); a
  pointer to another in-workspace path outside those trees, a pointer whose raw
  path traverses a mutable workspace child, or one into a writable mount, is
  rejected. Symlinks inside a nested `.git` are rejected. The root `.git` stays writable for Git;
  the file tools refuse any nested `.git` write. On Linux, every protected-path
  ancestor directory is pinned as a mountpoint; macOS emits entry-deny rules for
  the same ancestors, so they cannot be renamed around the read-only bind.
  `.gitmodules` is protected.
  `.git/hooks`, `.git/modules` and
  `.git/worktrees` are protected as roots but not recursively scanned (host-owned; a user hook symlink may target
  a workspace path, which remains writable). A symlinked `.git/hooks` directory
  itself is rejected at setup; replace it with a real directory. Nested `.gitattributes` files are
  not individually protected. On macOS, Seatbelt denies `file-link` to protected/denied paths;
  pre-existing hardlink aliases remain a limitation (see Known limitations).
- **Denied paths.** `deniedPaths` from the trusted file are hidden from the
  shell and refused by the tool guard for reads and writes, including files in
  system roots, missing paths resolved through the nearest existing ancestor,
  and broken final symlink targets. Existing files are masked; existing directories become empty tmpfs
  mounts, so writes there are ephemeral and never reach the host. A denied path
  that is a parent of a writable mount masks the child too. Relative paths
  resolve against the workspace. On Linux, a missing or broken target cannot be
  masked until it exists; the tool guard still denies it.
- **Unsandboxed commands.** Only exact `unsandboxedCommands` entries from the
  trusted file run on the host shell. A command containing `;`, `&`, `|`, a
  backtick, `$`, `(`, `)`, `<`, `>` or a newline never matches. A `prefix *`
  entry authorizes all arguments of that command; the command inherits the host
  environment and cwd. The shortcut is logged in `OSB_TRACE` by pattern index,
  never with the command or pattern text. This is an explicit user trust
  decision, not a sandbox boundary.
- **No host home.** `$HOME` is a synthetic directory inside the sandbox; the
  host home and `~/.ssh`/`~/.aws`/cloud credentials are not mounted (Linux) or
  are outside the read allowlist (macOS).
- **Workspace guards.** A real sandbox is only built when the workspace is a
  directory, not `/`, not the host home, not an ancestor of the host home and
  not a host system or credential directory. Extra mounts must exist, are
  canonicalised, and may not be `/`, the host home, an ancestor of it, a
  credential directory or a host system path when writable. Protected system
  roots include `/run` and `/var` subtrees; `/tmp`, `/var/tmp`,
  `/private/var/tmp`, `/var/folders`, `/private/var/folders` and `/var/www` are
  the explicit writable exceptions. `/var/www` is only a convenience
  exception: do not grant it if a host web server executes files from that
  tree, because a writable document root is host code execution outside the
  sandbox. Credential directories include `~/.ssh`, cloud stores, OpenCode's
  XDG stores and `~/Library/Application Support/opencode` on macOS. The same
  path cannot be both writable and readable; the workspace is always writable.
- **Mount precedence.** Mounts are applied from broad to narrow; a more
  specific path wins. A readable subdirectory is read-only even inside the
  workspace, while a readable ancestor does not make the workspace or a more
  specific writable child read-only. Contradictory configurations (the same
  path in both lists, or the workspace as readable) are rejected at setup. The
  same plan drives Linux bind order and the macOS last-matching Seatbelt rule.
- **Fail-closed.** A real sandbox is probed at startup, then the generated
  wrapper is executed with `-c 'exit 42'`. If the binary, generated profile,
  mount, shell, layout or hook registration fails, shell commands are refused
  (`mode: "enforce"`). A shell hook also covers the TUI terminal; the tool-hook
  fallback blocks every agent shell call. If the host exposes no hook surface
  at all, setup fails loudly. `mode: "permissive"` is an explicit opt-out that
  runs shell commands unsandboxed with a warning; when the shell sandbox cannot
  be installed it also skips the tool guard.
- **Trusted binary.** bwrap/sandbox-exec is resolved once from fixed
  root-owned, non-group/world-writable absolute paths. `PATH` shims cannot
  substitute an unsandboxing binary.
- **V2 permission fidelity.** The V2 hook replaces only the shell executable.
  `event.command` is untouched, so OpenCode evaluates permission rules and
  records history against the original command. The working directory is
  validated both in the hook and again by the wrapper using `pwd -P`.
- **Tool guard (V2).** File tools and `webfetch` are checked against the same
  workspace policy by a permission hook. This is a policy layer, not an OS
  boundary; see [Tool guard](#tool-guard-v2).
- **Working directory confinement.** The wrapper refuses to run when the real
  working directory is outside the workspace or an explicit mount, including
  after a symlink swap between validation and execution.
- **Capabilities and namespaces.** `--unshare-all`, `--cap-drop ALL`,
  `--die-with-parent`, `--new-session` are always set on Linux. Seatbelt
  confinement is inherited by every child process on macOS.
- **Platforms.** Linux and macOS are supported natively. Windows is supported
  through **WSL2** (the distro is a normal Linux host). Native `win32` fails
  closed with a WSL2 hint; it has no native backend in this package.
- **No secret audit log.** There is no command log. The optional `OSB_TRACE`
  JSONL is debug-only and records events and unsandboxed pattern indexes, not
  command text or pattern values.

## V1 adapter

V1 has no shell-executable hook, so `tool.execute.before` rewrites the command
string to invoke the same wrapper. The sandbox boundary is identical, but
OpenCode V1 parses the rewritten string for its own permission rules and
records it in history; command-level deny/ask rules on the original command
are therefore not preserved. This is an upstream API limitation, not a
sandbox escape. Use V2 for permission-rule fidelity. The same hook applies the
best-effort file guard (including `apply_patch`) and the initial `webfetch`
check; V1 has no redirect hook. The V1 terminal shell is not covered by the
tool hook.

## Tool guard (V2)

The shell sandbox is kernel-enforced; the tool guard is not. It is an
in-process permission hook for OpenCode's file tools and `webfetch`:

- `read`/`glob`/`grep` may touch the workspace, `writablePaths`,
  `readablePaths` and the read-only system runtime. Host temp and OpenCode's
  retained tool-output directory are not readable by default; add one to
  `readablePaths` if needed;
- `write`/`edit`/`patch` (and V1 `apply_patch`) may touch only the workspace
  and `writablePaths`; protected workspace config and `deniedPaths` are always
  refused, including when the path does not exist yet;
- `deniedPaths` are refused for reads as well;
- `webfetch` is allow, deny, or hostname-allowlisted, and OpenCode checks every
  redirect through the same hook;
- symlinks, including broken links, are resolved component by component before
  the policy check.

It protects against prompt injection and misconfigured permissions, not against
a compromised OpenCode process or a malicious plugin running in the same
process. The V1 `tool.execute.before` guard is best-effort and does not see
`webfetch` redirects. MCP, LSP, `websearch`, image generation and non-shell
subprocesses remain outside. `webfetch` defaults to `"allow"`; use `"deny"` or
a non-empty `webfetchAllowlist` when exfiltration is in scope.

## Known limitations

- The **shell service** is OS-sandboxed. On V2, file tools and `webfetch` are
  policy-guarded in-process; on V1 they are best-effort. MCP servers, LSP
  servers, formatters, `websearch`, the image-generation provider call,
  subagents' other tools and processes outside the shell service remain outside
  the OS boundary. Local image inputs and image URLs still go through the same
  `read`/`webfetch` policy. The tool guard is not a substitute for a
  whole-process sandbox when the threat includes a compromised OpenCode.
- The tool guard resolves symlinks but not hard links or a path swapped after
  the check. A same-process attacker able to race the check is out of scope.
  On Linux, protected paths are separate mounts, so a new hardlink across them
  fails. On macOS, the profile denies `file-link` to protected/denied paths,
  but pre-existing hardlink aliases remain a path-based limitation; use a
  whole-process sandbox for hostile code.
- OpenCode management tools that use the `edit` permission for paths outside
  the workspace, such as `worktree_remove`, are denied while the tool guard is
  enforced. Manage worktrees outside OpenCode or set `toolGuard: "off"` if that
  workflow is required.
- On a V2 build that exposes neither `ctx.permission.hook` nor `ctx.tool.hook`,
  the shell sandbox remains active but file tools cannot be guarded. The plugin
  logs this at startup; `toolGuard: "enforce"` is best-effort on such a host.
- On a V2 build that has the permission hook but no `ctx.tool.hook`, the
  `write`/`edit`/`patch` tools may open a target before the permission hook
  denies the write. The write itself is denied; the pre-read contents are not
  returned to the model.
- OpenCode's retained tool-output directory is **not** readable by the tool
  policy by default. Add it to `readablePaths` if you need truncated results;
  it may contain output from other sessions of the same user.
- OpenCode management tools that do not assert a permission, such as
  `worktree_create` and `session_move`, are outside the tool policy.
- OpenCode's project instruction/config loader (`AGENTS.md`,
  `.opencode/opencode.json`, project plugins) runs in the host process outside
  the tool guard. The read tool's `AGENTS.md` discovery is checked, but
  bootstrap and reload reads are not. Protected paths stop a **sandboxed
  command** from planting those files; a repository that already ships a
  malicious plugin or config is trusted code before this plugin loads. Use a
  whole-process sandbox for that threat.
- An OpenCode project config can **remove** a plugin before it runs
  (`"plugins": []` or `"-@hamzaabili/opencode-sandbox"`). No plugin can make
  itself non-removable today
  ([opencode#57687](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/57687)).
  Managed hosts can pin the plugin in `/etc/opencode/opencode.json`; for
  hostile repositories use a whole-process sandbox. The trusted policy limits
  what a loaded plugin may do, not whether it loads.
- On Linux, a protected or denied path that does not exist cannot be
  bind-mounted, so a shell command can create it. The tool guard still denies
  the file tools. On macOS, Seatbelt denies the write even when the path is
  missing. Create the file/directory before relying on the Linux gap being
  closed.
- On macOS, Seatbelt rules are path-based. The profile denies `file-link` to
  protected/denied paths and denies the `.git` and protected directory entries
  against rename, but pre-existing hardlink aliases and nested
  `.gitattributes` remain out of scope. Use a whole-process sandbox for hostile
  code on macOS. Linux pins protected entries as mounts, so a new cross-mount
  hardlink fails (`EXDEV`).
- The protected/denied sets are path-based on both platforms: pre-existing
  hardlinks or aliases outside the named paths are not detected.
- Existing nested `.git` entries inside the workspace are protected by a
  bounded scan; a `.git` pointer to another in-workspace path outside
  `.git/modules` is rejected. The root `.git` stays writable for Git. A nested
  `.git` created after setup remains a shell missing-path residual; a submodule
  not checked out at setup is the same class.
- When OpenCode is opened in a subdirectory of a repository, sibling submodules
  outside that workspace are repository content the sandbox cannot write; they
  are not individually protected and remain trusted-repository input.
- A submodule `.git` pointer that does not exist at setup is a missing protected
  path on Linux; the tool guard denies it, but the shell gap remains until it
  exists.
- A workspace with more than 50,000 entries (excluding `node_modules`) fails
  closed rather than skipping nested `.git` protection.
- An allowed `.git/modules` or `.git/worktrees` pointer target that does not
  exist at setup is the same Linux missing-path class; the tool guard denies
  writes, but the shell can create the target until it exists.
- A nested repository with its own checked-out submodules/worktrees is not
  supported; open it at its root.
- `.git/hooks` is protected as a root but not recursively scanned. If a user
  symlinks a hook into the workspace, that target is writable by the sandbox;
  keep hook targets outside the workspace.
- V1 replay tracking is bounded to keep memory small; a replay evicted from the
  bound is refused, never run unsandboxed.
- `unsandboxedCommands` runs the matching command on the host by explicit user
  decision. The matcher is conservative (no metacharacters, no chained
  commands), but the authorized command itself is not sandboxed. Keep the list
  narrow and review it.
- `deniedPaths` masks existing files/directories. A missing denied path is
  enforced by the tool guard only; the shell cannot be masked until it exists.
- V1 `webfetch` redirects are not covered by the tool guard; only the initial
  URL is checked.
- The `webfetch` tool checks every redirect through the permission hook. The
  `image_generate` tool checks its input image URL only once, then follows
  redirects internally; an allowed host can redirect an image URL to a host
  outside the allowlist. Use `webfetch: "deny"` when image URL exfiltration is
  in scope.
- Do not run OpenCode as root. The workspace and credential guard is scoped to
  the home of the user running OpenCode and the listed system roots; a
  root-run process broadens what is readable and writable, including other
  users' homes.
- bwrap and Seatbelt share the host kernel: this is isolation, not
  virtualization. A kernel exploit is out of scope.
- Linux mounts `/etc` read-only. World-readable files there (and the workspace
  itself) remain visible; do not place secrets in a world-readable `/etc` file
  or in the workspace.
- macOS read access is allowlisted to the system runtime, workspace, synthetic
  home and explicit readable paths; metadata (`stat`) is allowed
  globally so path resolution works. File contents outside the allowlist are
  denied. Host temp dirs are not visible; writes are limited to the workspace,
  synthetic home (including its tmp) and explicit writable paths. `TMPDIR`
  points at the synthetic home temp. The allowlist includes read-only system trees such as `/Library`,
  `/private/var/db`, `/opt` and `/usr/local`; they are not the host home, but
  they may contain application data or package-manager configuration.
- `network: "allow"` shares the whole host network. There is no shell-network
  domain allowlist and no TLS-intercepting proxy; use the OS firewall or a VM
  if you need per-host shell egress control. `webfetchAllowlist` filters the
  `webfetch` tool by hostname; it is not a proxy and does not govern shell
  egress.
- Explicit `writablePaths`, `readablePaths` and `passEnv` are trust decisions.
- Windows is unsupported and fails closed.
- The startup probe proves the sandbox can be created at load time. A later
  per-command failure is reported by the command itself (the wrapper exits
  non-zero); it is never silently retried unsandboxed.

## Reporting

Report vulnerabilities privately via GitHub's "Report a vulnerability" flow on
the repository. Do not open a public issue for a suspected sandbox escape.
